title: Factor Graphs and Network Integration
markdown: ## What this covers Only a slide deck survives for this lecture — no transcript, no notes, no problem set — so this chapter follows the deck's own order rather than reconstructing spoken motivation that was never captured. The question running through it is: once a cell's state is measured by several incompatible assays (copy number, expression, protein abundance, genetic-screen hits, protein interactions), how do you combine them into one model? The answer given is always some kind of **graph plus an algorithm that runs on it** — a factor graph and the sum-product algorithm, a Bayesian network over interaction evidence, or a weighted network searched by an optimization routine. It assumes familiarity with basic probability (joint distributions, marginals, Bayes' rule) and with the idea of a directed pathway diagram; it does not assume prior exposure to factor graphs or belief propagation, which the lecture introduces from scratch. ## Factor graphs and the sum-product algorithm A **factor graph** is a bipartite graph with two kinds of vertex: a **variable node** for each unknown quantity, and a **factor node** for each local function (each "piece") of a joint distribution that the overall probability factors into. An edge joins a variable to a factor exactly when that variable is an argument of that factor's function. This is the representation used throughout the rest of the lecture, so it is worth fixing the vocabulary before anything is built on top of it. When the factor graph is a tree, the **sum-product algorithm** ("belief propagation") computes *every* variable's marginal distribution simultaneously, by passing messages along the edges under one scheduling rule: **a vertex sends its message toward a neighbour only after it has received a message from every one of its other neighbours.** Root the tree anywhere and this says exactly what the section title says — messages flow up from the leaves first, since a leaf has no other neighbours to wait for. Two rules describe what a message actually is: - a **variable node** forwards to one neighbouring factor the *product* of the messages it has received from all its other neighbouring factors; - a **factor node** forwards to one neighbouring variable $x$ the **summary for $x$** — its function's local marginal, found by summing out every other variable in its scope — of the product of its own function with the messages it has received from its other neighbours. Running this sweep from every leaf to a root and back down again gives, at each variable, its exact marginal as the product of all the messages arriving there. The full recursion is due to Kschischang, Frey and Loeliger's 2001 paper on factor graphs and the sum-product algorithm, which the deck cites rather than re-derives. ## PARADIGM: pathway activity from a factor graph **PARADIGM** (Vaske et al., 2010) is a worked use of exactly this machinery on a real pathway. Each gene is modelled as a short chain of hidden **variable nodes** — gene copy number, expression state, protein level, protein activity — each connected to an **observed evidence node** from the assay that measures it: array CGH or SNP-chip data feeds the copy-number node, transcriptomics feeds the expression node. The chain is meant to capture, in order, transcriptional regulation, translational regulation and protein degradation, and intracellular/extracellular signalling. A worked toy example in the deck chains two such genes together: MDM2 (DNA to mRNA to protein to active protein) feeding into TP53 (the same four-stage chain) feeding into apoptosis. A more general version of the same idea, from Goldstein et al. (2013), names five variable types — genomic copy (G), epigenetic promoter state (E), mRNA transcript level (T), peptide/protein level (P), active protein (A) — connected by three regulation-edge types: transcriptional (RT), translational (RP) and post-translational (RA) — plus upstream and downstream gene–gene interaction edges. Circles denote variables and black squares denote factors throughout, exactly the factor-graph convention from the previous section. **Building the joint distribution.** A known pathway is first converted to a directed graph with each edge labelled positive or negative for its direction of influence. Each variable $x_i$ then gets one factor $\phi_i(x_i, \text{Parents}(x_i))$ built from an **expected state**, computed as a vote among its parents: - a parent connected by a positive edge contributes a vote equal to $+1$ times its own state; a parent connected by a negative edge contributes $-1$ times its own state; - parents connected by an edge labelled "minimum" are collapsed into a single AND-like vote equal to the *minimum* of their states; parents connected by an edge labelled "maximum" are collapsed into a single OR-like vote equal to the *maximum* of their states; - a vote of zero abstains; if there are no votes at all the expected state is $0$; otherwise the expected state is the majority vote, with a tie between $+1$ and $-1$ broken in favour of $-1$ (repressors and deletions are given the benefit of the doubt). The factor itself is a noisy match to that expected state: $$\phi_i(x_i, \text{Parents}(x_i)) = \begin{cases} 1-\epsilon & x_i \text{ is the expected state} \\ \epsilon/2 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ with $\epsilon$ set to $0.001$ in practice — so the matching state gets probability $0.999$ and each of the two non-matching states (variables take three values, $-1$/$0$/$1$) gets $0.0005$, and the three probabilities sum to one as they must. The full joint is the normalized product of every factor, $$P(X) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{j=1}^m \phi_j(X_j), \qquad Z = \prod_j \sum_{S \sqsubseteq X_j} \phi_j(S),$$ and a marginal or a data-conditioned likelihood is obtained the same way, restricting the sum in each factor to settings consistent with the fixed variable or with the observed data $D$: $$P(x_i = a \mid \Phi) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{j=1}^m \sum_{S \sqsubseteq A_i(a)\, X_j} \phi_j(S), \qquad P(x_i=a, D \mid \Phi) = \frac{1}{Z}\prod_{j=1}^m \sum_{S \sqsubseteq A_i(a)\cup D\, X_j} \phi_j(S).$$ This is exactly the sum-product computation of the previous section run over the whole pathway graph: each factor's inner sum is the "summary" message it sends toward the variable being conditioned on, and the outer product over factors is the variable collecting messages from all its neighbours — which is why the lecture opens with belief propagation before it ever mentions PARADIGM. Given per-sample copy-number and expression matrices, the goal is to estimate, for each gene $i$ and state $a\in\{-1,0,1\}$, the pathway-activity score $$L(i,a) = \log\frac{P(D,x_i=a\mid\Phi)}{P(D,x_i\ne a\mid\Phi)} - \log\frac{P(x_i=a\mid\Phi)}{P(x_i\ne a\mid\Phi)} = \log\frac{P(D\mid x_i=a,\Phi)}{P(D\mid x_i\ne a,\Phi)}.$$ The second line follows by Bayes' rule: each joint probability splits into a likelihood times a prior, and the two priors cancel against the subtracted term, leaving a pure likelihood ratio — a log-odds that the data favour state $a$ over any other state, with the gene's own prior tendency divided out. The factor probabilities $\phi_i$ (equivalently the model parameters) are fit by EM from the experimental data. ## Combining heterogeneous evidence into an interactome A different integration problem: instead of one pathway's hidden states, combine several independent kinds of evidence about whether two proteins interact at all. Jansen et al. (2003) route each evidence type through its own naive-Bayes or fully-connected Bayesian-network classifier and then combine the outputs: - in-vivo pull-down data (Gavin, Ho) and yeast two-hybrid data (Uetz, Ito) each go through a fully-connected Bayesian network to give a **PIE** score (physical interaction evidence); - mRNA co-expression, GO process annotation, MIPS functional annotation and gene essentiality each go through a naive-Bayes classifier to give a **PIP** score (process-based evidence); - PIE and PIP are combined by a further naive-Bayes step into **PIT**, the total probabilistic score for the interaction — the entries of the resulting **probabilistic interactome**. A later effort standardizes this kind of combination: PSICQUIC/PSISCORE (Aranda et al., 2011) define **MIscore**, a single number in $[0,1]$ built as a weighted combination of three sub-scores — the number of supporting publications $S_p(n)$, the experimental detection method $S_m(cv)$, and the annotated interaction type $S_t(cv)$ — each itself normalized to $[0,1]$: $$S_{MI} = \frac{K_p S_p(n) + K_m S_m(cv) + K_t S_t(cv)}{K_p + K_m + K_t},$$ with the weights $K_p, K_m, K_t$ tunable. Scores of this kind assemble into a single **weighted interactome** — an edge-weighted graph in which every interaction carries a confidence rather than being simply present or absent — which is the input to the network-mining methods that follow. ## Modules, and the prize-collecting Steiner tree Once there is a weighted interactome, the next question is how to pull a small, explanatory subnetwork out of it rather than working with the whole graph. Barabási et al. (2011) distinguish two notions of **module**: a **topological module** is locally dense — more edges among its own nodes than to the rest of the network — while a **functional module** is a set of nodes with a high density of shared functional annotation; the two need not coincide. Huang et al. (2013) pose the extraction problem as a **prize-collecting Steiner tree**. Each data point (a gene or protein with supporting evidence) carries a **prize** for being included; excluding a node instead costs a **penalty**, proportional to the size of its measured change (e.g. the absolute log fold change); and including an edge costs a price set by how unlikely that interaction is. A single parameter $\beta$ balances the node penalty against the edge cost: $$\sum_{v \notin T} \beta\,\text{penalty}(v) \;+\; \sum_{e \in T} \text{cost}(e).$$ The tree $T$ minimizing this trades off two failure modes: leaving out a node that really did change, versus dragging in a low-confidence edge just to connect two nodes that are individually worth including. The deck cites two optimization approaches to solving it (Biazzo, Braunstein and Zecchina, 2012; Ljubić et al., 2006), and contrasts the result with a **naive** alternative — simply taking, e.g., the 2,500–4,500 nearest network neighbours of the phosphoproteins and transcription factors of interest — which the deck presents as producing a much less specific network. One stated downstream use: rank every node in the interactome by its weighted distance to the Steiner tree, and read the ranking as a list of candidate **drug targets** — nodes close to the recovered subnetwork are proposed as high-priority targets, contrasted against a set of control targets ranked far lower. ## Why no single 'omic layer is enough Two pieces of evidence in the deck argue for combining layers rather than trusting any one assay on its own. **mRNA does not predict protein level.** de Sousa Abreu et al. (2009) report only a weak correspondence between mRNA and protein expression levels — $R^2 = 0.22$, Spearman $R_s = 0.46$ — across a roughly 1,000-fold range of protein concentrations. Ning et al. (2012) sharpen this: four different label-free mass-spectrometry-based protein quantification methods (SpectrumMill, msInspect, msBID, NSAF) correlate strongly with *each other*, in the range $0.84$–$0.92$, but each correlates with RNA-based measures (RPKM, microarray) only in the range $0.36$–$0.54$. The disagreement is not measurement noise inside one assay type; it is a real gap between mRNA level and protein level. **Genetic hits and expression changes barely overlap.** For a set of perturbations in yeast (hydroxyurea-induced growth arrest, MMS-induced DNA damage, cycloheximide, tunicamycin-induced ER stress, arsenic, oleate, and a median over 24 gene-inactivation datasets), the deck reports: | Perturbation | Differentially expressed genes | Genetic hits | Overlapping genes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Growth arrest (hydroxyurea) | 59 | 86 | 0 | | DNA damage (MMS) | 198 | 1448 | 43 | | Protein biosynthesis block (cycloheximide) | 20 | 164 | 0 | | ER stress (tunicamycin) | 200 | 127 | 5 | | ATP synthesis block (arsenic) | 828 | 50 | 9 | | Fatty acid metabolism (oleate) | 269 | 103 | 9 | | Gene inactivation (24 datasets, median) | 27 | 130 | 0 | A gene whose deletion produces the perturbation's phenotype is usually *not* one of the genes whose expression changes in response to it. Genetic screens are reported to be enriched for transcriptional regulators and signal-transduction genes, while expression changes are enriched for metabolic processes — two different, complementary readouts of the same perturbation, which is the case for building a network that connects them rather than intersecting the two gene lists directly. ## Case study: bridging genetic and transcriptional data with minimum-cost flow The deck works through one concrete pipeline (from a 2009 *Nature Genetics* paper, "Bridging high-throughput genetic and transcriptional data reveals cellular responses to alpha-synuclein toxicity") for turning that mismatch into a network. It builds the underlying graph from the protein interactome together with transcription-factor edges inferred from ChIP-chip binding data and sequence analysis, and shows one signalling cascade it is meant to recover — the yeast DNA-damage sliding-clamp checkpoint, MEC3–DDC1–RAD17–RAD24 sensing damage and signalling through MEC1 (the yeast ortholog of ATM) to RAD9, RAD53 (ortholog of CHK2), DUN1 and RFX1, producing cell-cycle arrest and DNA repair. **Test case.** Deleting *STE5* in the yeast pheromone-response pathway: 20 genes rescue the mating phenotype in a genetic screen (SGD), while only 12 genes are differentially expressed in the Rosetta compendium. The relevant pathway members are Ste2, Gpa1, Ste18, Ste4, Ste5, Ste11, Ste7, Cdc42, Ste20, Ste50, Fus3, Dig1 and Ste12. A **naive approach** — enumerate all interactome paths of length at most 3 connecting the genetic hits to the expression hits — returns a network of 193 nodes and 778 edges: technically connected, but far too large and unspecific to read as an explanation. The better approach treats each edge's reliability as a probability $P_{ij}$ (assigned from the same kind of Bayesian evidence-integration used earlier: Jansen et al., 2003; Myers et al., 2005) and looks for paths that **maximize the product of edge probabilities** along the path — equivalently, minimize the sum of $-\log P_{ij}$. This is exactly a **minimum-cost flow** problem: push flow from a source (the genetic hits) to a sink (the expression hits), with $$\text{cost}(e_{ij}) = f_{ij}\cdot(-\log P_{ij}), \qquad \min\Big(\sum \text{cost}(e_{ij}) - \gamma\sum f_{Sj}\Big),$$ where $f_{ij}$ is the flow on edge $e_{ij}$ and every edge has unit capacity $c_{ij}=1$. Flow routes preferentially along high-probability (low-cost) edges rather than sparse low-confidence ones, and each protein can then be ranked by how much flow passes through it — a measure of its importance to the perturbation. **Result.** The minimum-cost-flow network for the Ste5 test case has 49 nodes and 96 edges, and is enriched for the pheromone-response process at $p < 10^{-18}$ — a small, specific network in place of the naive method's 193-node, 778-edge tangle. ## A taxonomy of network models The deck's closing slide organizes everything above along two axes: whether the mechanism relating variables is known, and whether it is described in physical or in purely statistical terms. | | Known components | Unknown components | | --- | --- | --- | | **Physical relationships** | Differential equations; Boolean logic, decision trees | Interactome models | | **Statistical relationships** | Bayesian networks | Mutual information; regression, clustering | And a second summary, of what goes into a network model and what is done with it once built: - **Structure of the network**: coexpression, mutual information, physical/genetic interactions. - **Analysis of the network**: ad hoc inspection, shortest path, clustering, optimization (the Steiner-tree and minimum-cost-flow methods above are instances of the last). ## Sources - All content: the reconstructed slide deck for lecture 16 of MIT OCW 7.91J (*Foundations of Computational and Systems Biology*, Spring 2014), files `16-slides/01` through `16-slides/07`.
